effect_sizes.interpretation: On the full N=80 replication, Cohen's d_z = 0.0041 is a negligible effect size (< 0.05, well under even the 0.2 'small effect' convention) -- consistent with the TOST equivalence result below, not merely a non-significant p-value.

pilot_retrospective_design_analysis.note: Descriptive context ONLY. This uses the N=20 pilot's own observed effect size to compute the pilot's retrospective power, which is a circular statistic if treated as evidence (a non-significant pilot's own point estimate will almost always look 'underpowered' for itself). We report it only to motivate why a properly powered replication -- sized against a pre-specified effect, not this pilot's own noisy estimate -- was needed; the actual evidence for 'no meaningful interaction' comes from the TOST equivalence test and 95% CI on the N=80 replication below, not from this block.

equivalence_test_tost_n80.method: Two one-sided tests (TOST), paired t-test formulation
equivalence_test_tost_n80.sesoi_note: SESOI = Cohen's conventional 'small effect' boundary (d_z=0.20), used as a default in the absence of a domain-specific threshold; reported as a stated convention, not derived from the data.
equivalence_test_tost_n80.interpretation: The N=80 replication's mean interaction effect (0.0002) is statistically equivalent to zero within a small-effect bound (d_z=0.20, i.e. 0.0111 raw ARI units), p=0.04185. Unlike the pilot's retrospective power figure above, this directly tests (rather than merely fails to reject) the claim that any true interaction effect is too small to be practically meaningful.

confidence_interval_95pct_n80.interpretation: 95% CI for the true mean interaction effect: [-0.0121, 0.0125], a narrow interval straddling zero, consistent with the TOST equivalence result above.

ols_anova_decomposition.model: ari_k4 ~ intercept + B + C + B:C, OLS, N=80 (20 seeds x 4 configs)
ols_anova_decomposition.note: The B:C coefficient is the regression-based analogue of the interaction effect tested by the paired Wilcoxon test above; both approaches test the same qualitative hypothesis from different angles (nonparametric vs. parametric).

multiple_testing_correction.note: Only two tests target the same hypothesis in this study, so the correction has limited effect, but it is reported for completeness and statistical rigor rather than presenting two uncorrected p-values side by side.
